newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Talk of Indians, Nazis highlight Havel's Brazil tour.
newsitem.headline: Talk of Indians, Nazis highlight Havel's Brazil tour.

text.p: The president of the Czech Republic, Vaclav Havel, met Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Monday at the start of week-long tour highlighted by Indians, memories of the Nazis and trade.

On the first-ever visit to Latin America by a Czech head of state, Havel said he and Cardoso discussed bilateral economic ties and global issues, such as reform of the United Nations. The two intellectuals also exchanged books.
"This visit is of great importance to me. I want to strengthen our political, economic and cultural relations," Havel told reporters in the capital Brasilia.
The Czech president's visit to Brazil was aimed at improving commercial ties and investment between the two countries, whose bilateral trade in 1995 amounted to less than $100 million.
But officials from both sides said the personal similarities between the two presidents were likely to dominate headlines.

Havel is a poet turned leader after the 1989 "Velvet Revolution" which toppled the Communists in former Czechoslovakia. Cardoso was a left-wing sociologist who went into exile under Brazil's 1964-85 military regimes.
The Czech leader's itinerary was also full of offbeat cultural activities.

He was due to travel to the Amazon rainforest on Tuesday, where he will visit the jungle reserve of the Waimiri-Atroari Indians, a tribe that recently agreed to allow the government to build a controversial highway through its land.

Next Saturday Havel will pay a visit to the city of Lidice in the interior of Rio de Janeiro state, named after the Czech town that was destroyed by the Nazis in the Second World War in retaliation for a Czech partisan attack on a German general.

"We cannot forget that Brazil was one of those countries that contributed to the fall of the Nazis, being among the Allies in the Second World War," Havel said, adding that the mayor of Lidice was with him to pay his town's respects to its Brazilian namesake.
Czech Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy told reporters that several dozen businessmen travelling with the president would ensure economics was kept on the agenda.

He said the Czech concern Skoda was considering building a factory to make about 500 trucks a year and that negotiations were ongoing with eight Brazilian states. Dlouhy said he could not comment on the value of the potential investment.
The industry minister added that Prague was anxious to help Czech firms maintain their international reputation as exporters of high-quality machinery and that Brazil was an obvious market.
Havel was due to leave Brazil on Sept. 21 and head for Chile. After Chile he was scheduled to tour Argentina and Uruguay, two of Brazil's partners in the Mercosur customs union.
Havel will return briefly to Brazil for some sightseeing at the spectacular Foz de Iguacu waterfalls before flying back to Prague on Sept. 28.
